newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's Nazi gold probe extended to end of 1997.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Nazi gold probe extended to end of 1997.

text.p: An investigation into how much gold looted from Holocaust victims was accepted by Sweden during World War Two will now not be completed until the end of the year, Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, said on Tuesday.
A committee set up last December to examine the Riksbank's archives and reports on gold purchases from Germany during the war was to have concluded by late August.
"But the assignment has turned out to be more extensive and complicated than could have been expected from the start," the Riksbank said in a statement.
"Moreover the Commission on Jewish Assets in Sweden at the time of World War Two has recently requested some supplementary and extended work by the committee."
The bank had appointed three lawyers to investigate how much looted gold was accepted by the Riksbank and whether any remains in its vaults.
Sweden's policy during the war came under scrutiny following criticism of Swiss banks' dealings with Nazi Germany.
Both countries were neutral during the war but Sweden maintained extensive trade ties with Germany, selling up to 35 million tonnes of much-needed iron ore in return for gold.
German troops transited Sweden -- with official approval -- to neighbouring Norway, which was invaded.
Sweden only decided in March 1944, a year before the war ended and months before allied troops launched the invasion of France, to stop accepting German gold in return for iron ore.
Sweden returned about 13 tonnes of gold to Belgium and the Netherlands after the war when it was shown it had been looted by occupying Germans.
